questions.stem: The four stages of the software engineering project are:
options: Identifying and defining → research and planning → producing and implementing → testing and evaluating
questions.explanation: They are iterative — testing findings feed back into earlier stages rather than ending the process.

questions.stem: SMART requirements stand for:
questions.explanation: The point of SMART is that a requirement written this way can actually be tested later — "the system should be fast" cannot.

questions.stem: The difference between functional and performance requirements is:
options: Functional describes how well; performance describes what
Functional describes what the system must do; performance describes how well it must do it
Performance requirements apply only to hardware
questions.explanation: "Users can book a room" is functional; "the booking confirms in under 2 seconds under 500 concurrent users" is performance.

questions.stem: A project boundary is:
options: The invisible line separating the system being built from everything else, defining scope and expectations
A value at the edge of a valid range
questions.explanation: Note the same word means something different in testing — a boundary value sits exactly on the edge of an accepted range.

questions.stem: Feasibility in a project context asks whether:
options: The technology exists anywhere in the world
The project can realistically be completed within the available schedule and budget
questions.explanation: Schedule and budget are the two named dimensions; a feasibility answer that ignores both is incomplete.

questions.stem: A stakeholder is:
options: Anyone affected by or with an interest in the system — client, end-users, developers, management, regulators
questions.explanation: Missing a stakeholder is a classic cause of a solution that meets the specification but not the need — a validation failure.

questions.stem: A use case describes:
options: How a user interacts with the system to achieve a goal — actor, trigger, main sequence and alternative/error paths
questions.explanation: Use cases are used to derive functional requirements and to design test cases, which is why the error paths matter as much as the main sequence.

questions.stem: The four software implementation methods are:
questions.explanation: Do not confuse implementation methods (how you switch systems over) with development approaches (how you build).

questions.stem: Direct implementation is characterised by:
options: Fast and cheap, but high risk because there is no fallback
Rolling out to one site first
questions.explanation: Old system off, new system on, at a set moment. Defensible only where the consequence of failure is low.

questions.stem: Parallel implementation is the safest because:
options: The old system remains available as a fallback and outputs can be cross-checked
questions.explanation: Its cost is that it is expensive and doubles the workload for the transition period.

questions.stem: A payroll system handling irreplaceable financial data should use which implementation method?
questions.explanation: Parallel — The choice depends on consequence of failure, not on cost. Safety-critical or irreplaceable data → parallel; low-stakes internal tool on a tight budget → direct.

questions.stem: Pilot implementation means:
options: Introducing the system module by module
Trialling the full system with one group or site before full rollout
Running old and new together everywhere
questions.explanation: Issues are found and fixed at limited scale, and pilot users often become advocates for the wider rollout.

questions.stem: Phased implementation trades:
options: Lower risk for slower delivery and complexity managing the transition
questions.explanation: During the transition, temporary interfaces between old and new modules must be built and maintained.

questions.stem: Waterfall is most appropriate when:
options: Requirements are expected to change frequently
The client wants to see working software every two weeks
Requirements are stable and fully known, and thorough documentation is required
The team is inexperienced with the domain
questions.explanation: Its strengths are clear structure, milestones and documentation; its weakness is that change is expensive and problems found late are costly.

questions.stem: Agile delivers value through:
options: A single release at the end of the project
Short sprints producing working software with continuous user involvement
questions.explanation: The trade-off is that the final cost and scope are harder to predict — which is why fixed-price contracts sit awkwardly with Agile.

questions.stem: WAgile is:
options: A hybrid applying Waterfall's structured planning with Agile iteration at specific points
questions.explanation: Useful where an organisation needs up-front approval and documentation but wants iterative delivery within phases.

questions.stem: Scrum and Kanban differ because Scrum:
options: Uses a continuous board with WIP limits
Uses fixed-length sprints with planning, review and retrospective
questions.explanation: Kanban is continuous flow — a to do / in progress / done board governed by work-in-progress limits rather than sprint boundaries.

questions.stem: A sprint is typically:
options: 1–4 weeks producing a potentially shippable increment
questions.explanation: Bracketed by sprint planning at the start and a review plus retrospective at the end.

questions.stem: The product backlog differs from the sprint backlog because the product backlog:
options: Is maintained by the developers only
Holds everything not yet built, from which a slice is pulled into the current sprint
questions.explanation: In Kanban the equivalent is the 'to do' column, governed by WIP limits.

questions.stem: On a Gantt chart, dependencies are shown by:
questions.explanation: Tasks run down the left, time across the top, bar length shows duration, and links show which task must finish before another can start.

questions.stem: The critical path is:
options: The most expensive sequence of tasks
The tasks assigned to the most senior developer
The sequence of dependent tasks determining the shortest possible project duration
The tasks with the most float
questions.explanation: A delay to a critical-path task delays the whole project; a delay to a task with float may not.

questions.stem: Float (slack) in a schedule is:
options: The spare time a non-critical task has before it would delay the project
questions.explanation: Consuming all of a task's float promotes it onto the critical path.

questions.stem: In a Learner Hours PWA build, "build database schema → front-end integration" is critical because:
options: They are assigned to the same person
The front end has nothing to connect to until the schema exists — the dependency is genuine
questions.explanation: Criticality comes from dependency, not from cost or duration alone.

questions.stem: Which is a named collaboration tool for project work?
questions.explanation: Shared platforms for communication, file sharing and task tracking — with version control platforms serving as both a technical tool and evidence of process.

questions.stem: Quality assurance in a project requires:
options: Defining measurable quality criteria, checking continually against requirements, and addressing compliance and legislative requirements
Removing all defects before any code is written
questions.explanation: "Must load in under 2 seconds" and "must pass all specified test cases" are the kind of measurable criteria set early.

questions.stem: The three named communication issues in project work are:
options: Involving and empowering the client, enabling feedback, negotiating
questions.explanation: Feedback must be structured so it is both given and acted on — a review nobody responds to is theatre.

questions.stem: Balancing what a client wants against technical feasibility and ethical considerations is which named issue?
options: Responding appropriately to stakeholders — a social and ethical issue in project work
questions.explanation: It sits alongside working individually versus collaboratively, which raises division of labour, shared credit and dependency risk.

questions.stem: Outsourcing appears in this module as:
options: A named strategy for responding to development difficulties — bringing in outside expertise for a specific problem
questions.explanation: The other named strategies are searching online for a solution and collaborating with peers.

questions.stem: A Level 0 DFD (context diagram) shows:
options: The whole system as a single process with its external entities and data flows
questions.explanation: A Level 1 DFD explodes that single process into sub-processes and shows the data stores.

questions.stem: Balancing a DFD means:
options: Each level has the same number of processes
Each level preserves the total inputs and outputs of the level above
questions.explanation: Level 1 adds internal detail only — it never invents a new external input or output.

questions.stem: A black hole in a DFD is:
options: An external entity connected to another entity
A data store with no name
A process with inputs but no outputs
questions.explanation: Its mirror image, a miracle (grey hole), is output produced with no matching input.

questions.stem: A DFD shows:
options: The order in which processes execute
How data moves between processes, data stores and external entities
questions.explanation: DFDs show where data goes, not when. Sequence and decision logic belong on a flowchart.

questions.stem: In a structure chart, a filled circle on an arrow indicates:
questions.explanation: A control flag — Rectangles are modules, lines show calls, and labelled arrows show data passed down and results passed back.

questions.stem: A class diagram represents each class as a rectangle divided into:
questions.explanation: Inheritance is shown with a hollow triangle arrow pointing from the subclass to the parent.

questions.stem: A storyboard communicates:
options: A sequential visual representation of user interaction and screens
questions.explanation: It exposes missing steps in the user journey before any code is written, and communicates the experience to non-technical stakeholders.

questions.stem: A data dictionary documents each data item's:
options: Name, type, size/format, validation rules and purpose
questions.explanation: It is technical documentation that a future maintainer depends on, since the maintainer is rarely the original author.

questions.stem: Pseudocode is best described as:
options: Code that compiles but does nothing
An algorithm description in English-like statements with defined structural rules and keywords
A flowchart in text form only
questions.explanation: It lets the logic be reviewed independently of language syntax — and the 2025 paper asked candidates to convert pseudocode to Python.

questions.stem: The back end contributes to a project through all of the following except:
options: Robust error handling so the system fails gracefully
A well-designed API / data contract for the front end
questions.explanation: Security engineering is the fourth named contribution — building security into the back end protects the whole system.

questions.stem: Computational thinking in a project involves:
options: Organising data logically, decomposing problems, interpreting patterns, and designing and implementing algorithms
questions.explanation: It is the analytical method that makes a problem implementable by a human, machine or computer.

questions.stem: Programmed data backup in a project means:
options: Code-based routines that regularly back up data, supporting business continuity
questions.explanation: In the exam-safe Python subset, os and datetime with with open(...) are enough to demonstrate it — no external libraries required.

questions.stem: Using with open("data.txt", "r") as file: is preferred because:
options: The file is automatically closed even if an error occurs
questions.explanation: Modes: "r" read, "w" overwrite, "a" append. Using "w" where "a" was intended silently destroys the existing file.

questions.stem: Code optimisation means:
options: Removing comments to reduce file size
Modifying code or redesigning algorithms to improve execution speed, reduce memory use and enhance performance
questions.explanation: Language-dependent examples in Python: more efficient data structures, avoiding redundant computation, list comprehensions instead of repeated appends.

questions.stem: Naming conventions matter because:
options: They are required by the compiler
Consistent, meaningful identifiers make code readable and maintainable — a requirement, not a stylistic preference
questions.explanation: 2025 marker feedback penalised unclear structure and overly complex nested control structures where a simpler one would work.

questions.stem: A stub is:
options: Temporary code that calls a module so it can be tested
A placeholder with the correct name, parameters and return type but no real logic
questions.explanation: Its complement is a driver — temporary code that calls a module. Both let unit and integration testing begin before every component exists. The 2025 paper gave a function stub as stimulus.

questions.stem: A driver in testing:
options: Calls the module under test so it can be exercised before the rest of the system exists
Stands in for something the module calls
questions.explanation: Stub = called by the module; driver = calls the module.

questions.stem: Prototyping in a project is used to:
options: Build partial versions to test ideas and gather feedback before full implementation
questions.explanation: Users react far more usefully to something concrete than to an abstract requirements question.

questions.stem: User documentation differs from technical documentation because user documentation covers:
options: How to operate the system — guides and help text
questions.explanation: Technical documentation is the data dictionary, diagrams, code comments and API contracts — essential because the maintainer is rarely the original author.

questions.stem: Implementing version control in a project supports:
options: Tracking changes, collaboration and rollback — and provides evidence of process
questions.explanation: Rollback is what makes experimentation safe; the audit trail is what makes the process assessable.

questions.stem: Verification asks:
options: Are we building the right system?
Are we building the system right — does it match the specification?
questions.explanation: Validation asks whether it meets the actual need. A system can pass verification and fail validation — it does exactly what the spec said, and the spec was wrong.

questions.stem: Black box testing means:
options: Designing tests to exercise every internal path and branch
Testing performed by the developer who wrote the code
Checking outputs for given inputs without examining the code
questions.explanation: White box testing sees the code and designs tests to exercise specific paths, branches and loops.

questions.stem: Path testing ensures that:
options: Every logical path through the code executes at least once
questions.explanation: It is a white box technique — you cannot design path tests without seeing the code.

questions.stem: The three levels of testing, in order, are:
questions.explanation: Unit tests one function in isolation, integration checks that unit-tested components work together, and system tests the whole assembled application against the requirements.

questions.stem: The four categories of test data are:
questions.explanation: Testing one comfortably "normal" value does not score — specific, well-reasoned selection across all four does.

questions.stem: For a room booking system accepting 8am–6pm, which are boundary values?
questions.explanation: Exactly on the edge and just outside — where errors are most likely. Normal is 10:00am; invalid is "lunchtime"; extreme is 3:00am or the year 9999.

questions.stem: Invalid test data is used to confirm that:
options: Validation and error handling actually work — the input is rejected with a clear message
The system does not crash under load
questions.explanation: Extreme data — far beyond the expected range — is what confirms the system does not crash.

questions.stem: A test plan should document:
options: What will be tested, how, and the expected result to compare against actual output
questions.explanation: Comparing actual output with expected output is the fundamental test of correctness; any discrepancy is a defect to investigate.

questions.stem: A logic error is distinguished from a syntax error because a logic error:
options: Runs perfectly and produces the wrong answer
questions.explanation: A syntax error breaks the language's rules so the program will not run; a runtime error crashes during execution. Logic errors are the hardest to find because nothing reports them.

questions.stem: Dividing by zero at run time produces:
questions.explanation: Runtime error — the program crashes during execution. Opening a missing file is another example.

questions.stem: Debugging differs from testing because debugging:
options: Locates and fixes the cause of a defect already detected
questions.explanation: Techniques: read the error message and traceback, add print/log statements, use breakpoints and step through, and isolate with a minimal test case.

questions.stem: Evaluating effectiveness requires:
options: Comparing performance against the measurable criteria defined earlier, with evidence, and making a judgement
questions.explanation: Structure: state the criterion → state the evidence → make a judgement → note the limitation → recommend the improvement.

questions.stem: Feedback gathered during evaluation should be:
options: Synthesised into a report, analysed, and incorporated into revisions
questions.explanation: Evaluation that never changes a decision is documentation, not evaluation.

questions.stem: A client's requirements are expected to evolve as they see the product. The best-justified approach is:
options: Agile, because short iterations with continuous client involvement absorb change cheaply
questions.explanation: Justify by naming the criterion (requirement stability) and saying why the alternative is worse — Waterfall makes late change expensive because everything downstream must be reworked.

questions.stem: A team chooses Agile but the client is unavailable for feedback for the whole term. The likely outcome is:
options: Agile works better without client input
The core benefit — continuous validated feedback — is lost, and the team builds on assumptions in short bursts
questions.explanation: Approach selection must account for the client's capacity, not only the team's preference.

questions.stem: A hospital medication system passes every unit and integration test but nurses say it does not fit their workflow. This is:
options: A validation failure — the specification did not reflect the real need
questions.explanation: Trace it back to identifying and defining — requirements were probably gathered from managers rather than from the actual end-users.

questions.stem: A project is two weeks late on a task with three weeks of float. The correct response is:
options: Recognise the end date is not yet affected, but monitor — the task has consumed most of its slack and is close to becoming critical
Add developers to the critical path
questions.explanation: Float is precisely the amount of delay a non-critical task can absorb before it starts to matter.

questions.stem: A client requests three extra features mid-project with no change to deadline or budget. The best response is:
options: Assess and document the time and cost impact, present options — extend, re-prioritise, or defer — and get agreement in writing
questions.explanation: Making the trade-off visible keeps the decision with the client. Cutting testing to fit is how projects fail quietly.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart shows all tasks at 100% complete but system testing has not begun. This most likely indicates:
options: Testing was never scheduled as work with duration and owners, or progress is being reported inaccurately
The critical path was too short
questions.explanation: Testing and evaluation is a project stage, not something that happens after the work.

questions.stem: A student project must demonstrate management and documentation of development. The strongest evidence is:
options: A Gantt chart showing planned versus actual, a version control history, and a dated log of decisions with their justification
questions.explanation: Planned versus actual on both time and scope is the core evidence of managed development rather than development that merely happened.

questions.stem: For a scenario with Student and ScholarshipStudent classes, the class diagram should show:
options: A dashed line with no arrow
A hollow triangle arrow from ScholarshipStudent to Student
questions.explanation: Inheritance arrows point from the subclass to the parent, and the triangle head is hollow. Markers reward correct standard notation explicitly.

questions.stem: Converting the pseudocode IF hours >= 120 THEN eligible = TRUE ELSE eligible = FALSE to Python, the most defensible version is:
questions.explanation: => is not a Python operator, THEN/TRUE are not Python keywords, and Python is case-sensitive (True, not true). The boolean assignment is also simpler than an if/else — favour clarity.

questions.stem: Which Python fragment would fail in the exam editor?
questions.explanation: The editor is locked down to the standard library — math, random, os and datetime. No pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib or scikit-learn, and no internet access.

questions.stem: A candidate calls calculate_total() on line 3 and defines it on line 20. The result is:
options: A syntax error at compile time
A NameError — the function must be defined before it is called at run time
questions.explanation: Calling a function before it is defined was explicitly named in 2025 marker feedback as a cause of lost marks, alongside incorrect indentation.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest set of test data for a login field accepting 6–12 characters?
options: "abcdef" and "abcdefghijkl" (boundaries), "abcde" and "abcdefghijklm" (just outside), "secure99" (normal), "" and a 5000-character string (extreme)
questions.explanation: All four categories, with a documented expected result for each. This level of specificity is what scores.

questions.stem: A team must decide between building in-house and outsourcing a payment module. The strongest justification structure is:
options: State criteria — internal capability, timeline, security and compliance obligations, cost, and long-term maintenance — evaluate both, then say why the rejected option is worse
questions.explanation: For payments specifically, PCI-DSS compliance is usually the deciding criterion — say so rather than leaving it implicit.

questions.stem: A system meets every requirement but users make frequent errors. The appropriate response is:
options: Add more training material and move on
Treat it as a design signal — usability test to find the cause, modify the design, then regression test
questions.explanation: "Modifying designs to improve functionality" is an explicit part of the testing and evaluating stage.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches stage to artefact?
options: Research and planning → DFDs, storyboards and the development approach decision
questions.explanation: Requirements, feasibility and boundaries belong to identifying and defining; the Gantt chart and modelling tools to research and planning.

questions.stem: A team writes the requirement "the app should be fast and easy to use". The best rewrite is:
options: "A logged-in user can record a driving session in under 30 seconds, and the dashboard loads in under 2 seconds on a 4G connection."
questions.explanation: Specific, measurable and time-bound — and therefore testable later, which is the entire point of SMART.

questions.stem: Which risk most justifies parallel over direct implementation for a school's reporting system at report time?
options: A failed cutover during report writing would leave teachers unable to complete legally required reports, with no fallback
The new system uses a different colour scheme
questions.explanation: Consequence of failure, and its timing, drive the decision — the same system might justify direct implementation in the January holidays.

questions.stem: In a DFD for a booking system, an arrow drawn directly from the CUSTOMER entity to the BOOKINGS data store is:
options: An error — data must flow through a process
questions.explanation: Along with black holes, miracles, unlabelled flows and store-to-store flows, this is one of the standard DFD errors markers look for.

questions.stem: The best reason to produce a storyboard before coding a PWA interface is:
options: It exposes missing steps in the user journey and communicates the experience to non-technical stakeholders while change is still cheap
questions.explanation: Change costs almost nothing on paper and a great deal after implementation — the same shift-left logic as secure design.

questions.stem: A project's evaluation reports only that "the client was happy". The weakness is:
options: There is no measurement against pre-defined criteria and no evidence — satisfaction is one criterion among several
questions.explanation: Add functional coverage against requirements, performance measurements, test results, accessibility conformance and usability data.

questions.stem: Which is the correct relationship between unit, integration and system testing?
options: They build on each other: units are tested in isolation, then together, then the whole assembled system against the requirements
questions.explanation: Integration testing assumes the units already pass — which is why stubs and drivers exist, so testing can start before every component is finished.

questions.stem: A developer fixes a defect and ships without re-running earlier tests. The risk is:
options: A regression — the change may have broken previously working functionality with nothing to detect it
The documentation will be out of date
The Gantt chart will be inaccurate
questions.explanation: Re-running the existing suite after every change is what makes an automated test suite pay for itself.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates the justify verb on an implementation method?
options: "Parallel implementation was used because the payroll data is irreplaceable and a failed cutover would prevent staff being paid; direct was rejected as it offers no fallback, and phased was rejected because payroll cannot be run half in each system."
"Parallel implementation runs both systems at once."
questions.explanation: Decision, reasons, evidence, and explicit rejection of the alternatives — that last element is what "justify" specifically demands.

questions.stem: A team's requirements come only from the school principal, not from the students who will use the system. The predictable outcome is:
options: A solution that meets the specification but not the need — a validation failure caused by missing a stakeholder
questions.explanation: Stakeholders are anyone affected by the system, and requirements gathered from only one of them will be incomplete.

questions.stem: In Kanban, a WIP limit exists to:
options: Limit how many items are in progress at once, exposing bottlenecks and improving flow
questions.explanation: Kanban has no sprints — flow is continuous, and WIP limits are the mechanism that replaces the sprint boundary as a constraint.

questions.stem: A structure chart shows module CalculateFee passing a value back to ProcessBooking. This is drawn as:
options: A labelled arrow indicating data returned upward
questions.explanation: Data passed down and results passed back up are both labelled arrows; a filled circle specifically denotes a control flag.

questions.stem: The strongest argument for writing technical documentation during development rather than after is:
options: Decisions and rationale are fresh, and maintenance — usually by someone other than the author — is the longest phase of the lifecycle
It makes the code run faster
questions.explanation: Documentation written months later reconstructs what the code does but loses why it does it that way.

questions.stem: A project encounters an unfamiliar technical problem. The named strategies for responding are:
options: Extend the deadline, reduce scope, cancel
Searching online for a solution, collaborating with peers, and outsourcing for specific expertise
questions.explanation: All three should be recorded in the project log with the decision and its reasoning — that record is assessable evidence.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question asking you to evaluate a developed solution, the weakest structure is:
options: A description of each feature the solution contains
Measured results compared against the original SMART requirements
A balanced discussion followed by a conclusion
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the single most common way to lose marks on an extended-response question.

questions.stem: For a solution you developed, the most convincing evidence of quality assurance is:
options: Measurable criteria defined at the start, a continual checking process against requirements during development, and documented compliance with privacy and accessibility obligations
questions.explanation: Note that QA is continual checking, not a final inspection.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce the risk that a late-discovered defect derails the project. The most effective structural change is:
options: Testing continuously from the start — unit tests alongside development, integration as components land — so defects are found while they are cheap
Adding more developers near the end
questions.explanation: The same shift-left cost argument that drives secure development drives test scheduling.

questions.stem: The clearest sign that a requirement is not SMART is:
options: It cannot be objectively tested as met or unmet
questions.explanation: If you cannot design a test for it, you cannot evaluate the finished system against it.

questions.stem: A project's DFD Level 1 introduces a new external entity that does not appear at Level 0. This is:
options: A balancing error — Level 1 may only add internal detail, never a new external input or output
questions.explanation: Balancing means each level preserves the total inputs and outputs of the level above.

questions.stem: Which statement about iterative development is most accurate?
options: It means repeating the same work
A project is divided into smaller parts developed incrementally, each iteration building on the previous
It removes the need for planning
questions.explanation: It is what allows feedback to change the product before it is too expensive to change.

questions.stem: A stimulus describes a small internal tool with a tight budget and low consequence of failure. The best-matched implementation method is:
questions.explanation: Direct — Right-sizing the method to the risk is the judgement being tested — the same reasoning that rules direct implementation out for payroll.

questions.stem: When a question gives a scenario, the single most valuable thing you can do is:
options: Give a technically correct general answer
Reference the specific system, data or user group in the stimulus in every point you make
questions.explanation: Ignoring the stimulus is the single most-cited marker complaint across all four modules.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes testing from evaluating?
options: Testing is done by the client
Testing establishes whether the system behaves correctly; evaluating judges whether it is effective against the criteria and the original need
questions.explanation: Testing is largely a verification activity; evaluation is largely a validation and effectiveness judgement.

questions.stem: The most defensible way to demonstrate that a solution met its purpose is:
options: A screenshot of the finished interface
Reporting each original SMART requirement against measured results — e.g. "dashboard loads in 1.4 s against a 2 s target; session logging completes in 22 s against a 30 s target"
questions.explanation: Closing the loop back to the requirements set at the start is what turns a description into an evaluation.

questions.stem: Across the whole project, the strongest evidence of professional practice is:
options: Planned versus actual tracking, version control history, documented decisions with reasoning, criteria-based evaluation, and demonstrated response to feedback
questions.explanation: These are exactly the things SE-12-09 asks you to apply methods to manage and document — and they are assessable in a way that a finished artefact alone is not.
